items.description: Analyze repository structure and existing research infrastructure
items.acceptance_criteria: Document listing all modules (.archivara/semantic_scholar.py, .archivara/concept_evolve.py, TASK_orchestrator.md), their purposes, interdependencies, and available tooling (Semantic Scholar API wrapper, concept evolution sub-agents). Include notes on figures/ and results/ output directories.

items.description: Conduct comprehensive web-based literature review on SSSP algorithms and recent breakthroughs
items.acceptance_criteria: Search the web for at least 15 relevant papers spanning: (1) classical SSSP (Dijkstra 1959, Fredman-Tarjan 1987 Fibonacci heaps, Thorup 1999 linear-time undirected), (2) recent breakthroughs (DMMSY STOC 2025 O(m log^{2/3} n) sorting barrier, Duan-Mao Feb 2026 O(m sqrt(log n)) directed, Bernstein-Nanongkai-Wulff-Nilsen FOCS 2022 negative-weight near-linear, Haeupler-Rozhoň-Tarjan FOCS 2024 universal optimality), (3) related techniques (Pettie-Ramachandran 2005 undirected hierarchy, Bringmann-Cassis-Fischer 2023 improved negative-weight). Produce a structured summary document with each paper's key result, technique, and relevance to the research goal.

items.description: Create and maintain sources.bib with BibTeX entries for all consulted sources
items.acceptance_criteria: sources.bib file exists in repo root with valid BibTeX entries for at least 12 relevant papers. Must include entries for: Fredman-Tarjan 1987, Thorup 1999, Pettie-Ramachandran 2005, Bernstein-Nanongkai-Wulff-Nilsen 2022, Duan-Mao-Shu-Yin FOCS 2023, Haeupler-Hladik-Rozhoň-Tarjan-Tětek FOCS 2024, Duan-Mao-Mao-Shu-Yin STOC 2025, Duan-Mao 2026, and at least 4 additional relevant works. Each entry must have author, title, year, venue/journal, and DOI/arXiv ID where available.

items.description: Formalize the computational model, problem definition, and known lower bounds
items.acceptance_criteria: Written document specifying: (1) the comparison-addition model (only comparisons and additions on real edge weights allowed), (2) formal SSSP problem definition on directed graphs G=(V,E,w) with non-negative real weights, (3) the Ω(n log n) sorting lower bound and why it was believed to apply to SSSP, (4) how DMMSY circumvents the sorting barrier by avoiding full distance ordering, (5) the Haeupler et al. 2024 result showing Dijkstra IS optimal if distance ordering is required, and (6) known conditional lower bounds and open questions about achieving O(m) for directed SSSP.

items.description: Deep technical analysis of the DMMSY interval-pivot recursive decomposition technique
items.acceptance_criteria: Technical analysis document covering: (1) the frontier-size reduction insight — why Dijkstra's Θ(n) frontier is the bottleneck, (2) the recursive subproblem decomposition via interval pivots, (3) the Batch Prepend data structure on block-based linked lists, (4) how partial ordering replaces full sorting, (5) the specific recurrence yielding O(m log^{2/3} n), and (6) how Duan-Mao 2026 further improved this to O(m sqrt(log n)) by refining the decomposition. Must cite specific sections/lemmas from the papers.

items.description: Identify open theoretical gaps and candidate directions for further improvement
items.acceptance_criteria: Document listing at least 5 concrete candidate directions for improving beyond O(m sqrt(log n log log n)), with for each: (a) the specific technical obstacle, (b) why current techniques fall short, (c) what new idea might help, and (d) potential asymptotic target. Directions must include at least: tighter recursive decomposition, novel data structures for batch relaxation, exploiting graph structure (planarity, bounded treewidth, separator hierarchies), randomization vs determinism tradeoffs, and connections to other problems (MST, APSP, negative-weight SSSP). Reference prior work from sources.bib.

items.description: Implement Dijkstra's algorithm with Fibonacci heap as primary baseline
items.acceptance_criteria: Working implementation of Dijkstra + Fibonacci heap in Python or C++ that: (1) correctly solves SSSP on directed graphs with non-negative real weights, (2) passes correctness tests on at least 5 hand-crafted graphs including edge cases (single vertex, disconnected components, zero-weight edges, dense/sparse), (3) empirically demonstrates O(m + n log n) scaling, and (4) includes instrumentation to count comparisons and additions separately.

items.description: Implement a simplified DMMSY-style frontier reduction algorithm as advanced baseline
items.acceptance_criteria: Working implementation of a simplified version of the DMMSY recursive decomposition that: (1) correctly solves SSSP, (2) demonstrates sub-O(m + n log n) comparison count on sparse graphs (m = O(n)), (3) includes instrumentation counting comparisons, additions, and recursive depth, (4) passes the same correctness test suite as item_007. Reference the open-source C/Rust/Zig implementations on GitHub for guidance.

items.description: Design and implement benchmark graph generators covering diverse graph families
items.acceptance_criteria: Graph generator module producing at least 8 graph families: (1) Erdős-Rényi random G(n,p), (2) sparse random with m=O(n), (3) dense random with m=Θ(n²), (4) grid/lattice graphs, (5) scale-free/power-law (Barabási-Albert), (6) road-network-like planar graphs, (7) worst-case graphs for Dijkstra (adversarial frontier size), (8) layered DAGs. Each generator accepts n, m (or density), weight distribution parameters. Outputs adjacency list format. Generates graphs from n=100 to n=1,000,000.

items.description: Establish performance metrics framework with operation counting and wall-clock timing
items.acceptance_criteria: Metrics framework that captures: (1) comparison count, (2) addition count, (3) total operations in comparison-addition model, (4) wall-clock time with high-resolution timer, (5) memory usage (peak RSS), (6) recursive call depth (for decomposition-based algorithms). Framework produces structured JSON output per run. Includes statistical aggregation (mean, median, std, min, max) over multiple runs. Validates that comparison counts match theoretical predictions within 10% on known graph families for Dijkstra baseline.

items.description: Profile baselines to identify computational bottlenecks and guide novel algorithm design
items.acceptance_criteria: Profiling report covering both Dijkstra and DMMSY baselines on at least 4 graph families (sparse random, dense random, grid, scale-free) at sizes n=10K, 100K, 1M. Report must include: (1) breakdown of time spent in heap operations vs edge relaxation vs overhead, (2) comparison count as a function of n and m with fitted curves, (3) identification of the specific operations/phases consuming >20% of total work, (4) concrete observations about where the DMMSY approach gains over Dijkstra and where overhead cancels theoretical advantage. Reference the experimental analysis by [arXiv:2511.03007] showing Dijkstra's practical superiority due to DMMSY's large constants.

items.description: Develop theoretical framework for novel SSSP algorithm exploiting identified gaps
items.acceptance_criteria: Written theoretical framework document that: (1) selects and justifies one or more improvement directions from item_006, (2) proposes a specific algorithmic strategy with pseudocode, (3) explains how it differs from both Dijkstra and DMMSY, (4) identifies the key new idea or data structure that enables improvement, (5) states a conjectured time complexity strictly better than O(m sqrt(log n log log n)) with reasoning for why the bound should hold. Must reference and build upon at least 5 papers from sources.bib.

items.description: Design novel data structure or algorithmic primitive enabling the improvement
items.acceptance_criteria: Formal specification of a new data structure or algorithmic primitive that: (1) has clearly defined operations with stated time bounds, (2) supports the specific access pattern required by the novel SSSP algorithm, (3) improves upon existing structures (Fibonacci heap, DMMSY block-linked-list with Batch Prepend) for the targeted use case, (4) includes pseudocode for all operations, (5) has a correctness argument for each operation. If the primitive is a modification of an existing structure, clearly state what is new and why the modification yields better bounds.

items.description: Prove correctness of the novel SSSP algorithm
items.acceptance_criteria: Formal correctness proof containing: (1) a loop invariant or inductive argument showing that all computed distances are shortest-path distances, (2) a termination argument, (3) handling of all edge cases (unreachable vertices, zero-weight edges, ties), (4) proof that the data structure invariants from item_013 are maintained throughout execution. Proof must be written in a style suitable for a theoretical CS conference submission (lemma-proof structure with clear theorem statement).

items.description: Derive and prove the asymptotic complexity bound for the novel algorithm
items.acceptance_criteria: Complete complexity analysis showing: (1) a recurrence relation or amortized analysis for the total number of comparisons and additions, (2) solution of the recurrence yielding an explicit big-O bound, (3) the bound is strictly o(m sqrt(log n log log n)) — i.e., asymptotically better than the current best (Duan-Mao 2026) on at least one regime of m and n, (4) separate analysis for sparse (m=O(n)) and dense (m=Θ(n²)) cases, (5) clear statement of computational model assumptions. The proof must be self-contained and reference specific lemmas.

items.description: Implement the novel SSSP algorithm with full instrumentation
items.acceptance_criteria: Working implementation that: (1) correctly solves SSSP on all test graphs from item_007's test suite, (2) includes comparison/addition counting matching the metrics framework from item_010, (3) is well-documented with comments mapping code to pseudocode from item_012, (4) handles graphs up to n=1,000,000 without memory errors, (5) produces deterministic output (or seeds randomness if randomized). Code must be modular with the novel data structure from item_013 as a separate, testable component.

items.description: Verify implementation correctness against baseline on extensive random tests
items.acceptance_criteria: Correctness verification passing: (1) at least 1000 random directed graphs across all 8 families from item_009 with n ranging from 10 to 100,000, (2) exact agreement of computed distances with Dijkstra baseline on every test (within floating-point tolerance of 1e-9 for real weights, exact for integer weights), (3) zero failures across all tests, (4) log of all test configurations and results saved to results/ directory. Any discrepancy must be investigated and resolved before proceeding.

items.description: Optimize implementation for practical constant factors and cache performance
items.acceptance_criteria: Optimized implementation that: (1) reduces wall-clock time by at least 30% compared to initial implementation from item_016 on large graphs (n >= 100K), (2) documents specific optimizations applied (memory layout, branch prediction, cache-friendly traversal, allocation reduction), (3) addresses the practical overhead concerns raised in arXiv:2511.03007 about DMMSY implementations, (4) maintains correctness (re-passes full test suite from item_017).

items.description: Run comprehensive synthetic benchmarks comparing novel algorithm against all baselines
items.acceptance_criteria: Benchmark results on all 8 graph families from item_009 at sizes n={1K, 10K, 100K, 500K, 1M} with at least 3 density levels each. For each configuration: (1) comparison count, (2) addition count, (3) wall-clock time, (4) memory usage. At least 5 runs per configuration for statistical significance. Results saved as structured JSON in results/ directory. Total benchmark suite covers at least 200 distinct (family, n, density) configurations.

items.description: Evaluate on real-world or real-world-proxy graph instances
items.acceptance_criteria: Benchmarks on at least 4 real-world or real-world-proxy graphs: (1) road network (e.g., from DIMACS challenge or OpenStreetMap extract), (2) social network graph, (3) web graph, (4) biological/infrastructure network. For each: report comparison count, wall-clock time, and memory vs all baselines. If real datasets are unavailable, generate realistic proxies with matching degree distribution, diameter, and clustering coefficient, documenting the proxy methodology.

items.description: Perform comparative analysis against prior work with statistical rigor
items.acceptance_criteria: Comparison table and analysis showing: (1) operation count ratios (novel/Dijkstra, novel/DMMSY) across all tested configurations, (2) geometric mean speedup across all benchmarks, (3) statistical significance tests (paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank) for operation count differences, (4) identification of graph families and density regimes where the novel algorithm provides the largest/smallest improvement, (5) explicit comparison against theoretical predictions from item_015. Results must reference specific prior work from sources.bib.

items.description: Scalability analysis: empirical growth rate fitting across graph sizes
items.acceptance_criteria: Scalability analysis containing: (1) log-log plots of comparison count vs n for fixed m/n ratios, (2) fitted empirical growth curves with R² values, (3) comparison of empirical growth exponents against theoretical O-bounds for all three algorithms (Dijkstra, DMMSY, novel), (4) crossover point analysis — the minimum n at which the novel algorithm's operation count is lower than Dijkstra's, (5) extrapolation to n=10M and n=100M. All plots saved to figures/ directory.

items.description: Memory usage and auxiliary space analysis
items.acceptance_criteria: Memory analysis showing: (1) peak memory usage as a function of n and m for all three algorithms, (2) auxiliary space beyond the input graph, (3) comparison of memory overhead ratios, (4) analysis of whether the novel algorithm's space complexity is O(m+n) or requires super-linear space, (5) cache miss analysis if profiling tools are available. Document any space-time tradeoffs inherent in the novel approach.

items.description: Generate publication-quality figures for all experimental results
items.acceptance_criteria: At least 6 figures saved in figures/ directory: (1) operation count comparison bar chart across graph families, (2) scalability log-log plot with fitted curves, (3) speedup heatmap (graph family × density), (4) memory usage comparison, (5) empirical vs theoretical growth rate overlay, (6) crossover point visualization. All figures must have labeled axes, legends, consistent color scheme, and be suitable for inclusion in a conference paper (vector format PDF or high-res PNG at 300+ DPI).

items.description: Write comprehensive research report with full technical exposition
items.acceptance_criteria: Research report of at least 3000 words containing: (1) Abstract summarizing the result, (2) Introduction with motivation and context referencing DMMSY STOC 2025, Haeupler et al. FOCS 2024, and Bernstein et al. FOCS 2022, (3) Preliminaries section formalizing the model, (4) Algorithm description with pseudocode, (5) Correctness proof (from item_014), (6) Complexity analysis (from item_015), (7) Experimental evaluation summarizing results from Phase 4, (8) Related work section citing all papers from sources.bib, (9) Conclusion. Report must be structured for potential submission to a top-tier venue (STOC/FOCS/SODA).

items.description: Document limitations, assumptions, and open problems for future work
items.acceptance_criteria: Limitations section covering: (1) computational model assumptions and whether results extend to word-RAM model, (2) constant factor analysis — is the novel algorithm practically competitive or only theoretically superior, (3) restrictions on graph class (does the improvement hold uniformly or only for specific density regimes), (4) comparison with the universal optimality result of Haeupler et al. — does the novel algorithm require distance ordering, (5) at least 3 concrete open problems for future work, each with a clear problem statement and brief discussion of why current techniques are insufficient.

items.description: Prepare complete reproducibility package
items.acceptance_criteria: Reproducibility package containing: (1) README with step-by-step instructions to reproduce all results, (2) requirements.txt or equivalent dependency specification, (3) Makefile or script that runs the full experiment pipeline end-to-end, (4) all random seeds documented and hardcoded for deterministic reproduction, (5) expected output checksums or reference results for validation, (6) all code, data generators, and analysis scripts committed to the repository. A fresh clone of the repo must be sufficient to reproduce all figures and tables.

items.description: Final review: verify all acceptance criteria are met and sources.bib is complete
items.acceptance_criteria: Checklist verification that: (1) sources.bib contains at least 12 papers with complete BibTeX metadata, (2) all figures referenced in the report exist in figures/, (3) all experimental data exists in results/, (4) correctness tests pass with zero failures, (5) the claimed complexity bound is clearly stated and proven, (6) the research report is internally consistent (claims in abstract match results in evaluation), (7) the novel algorithm demonstrably improves upon O(m + n log n) in the comparison-addition model on directed graphs with non-negative real weights.
